author: buchanan_robert
text:
The snow had fallen all night long, and when they came
Out on the hill at noon one tree had caught the sun,
Had turned itself into a blazing globe of gold,
With fiery drops hanging from its limbs like fruit,

While the others, as they leaned out toward the sky,
Seemed heavy with their burden of thick white fleece,

Like old women who have dropped off weight.

author: cushag
text:
There are voices which never cease to sing
In every land where men have wandered yet,
Through all their homes, from one end of the earth
To other ends, from star to star’s extreme;
They echo down through time and change and death,
Though men may go or come, though things be gone.
The grass is greener on the mountain side,
The sunbeams slant more softly when we die;
We feel no pain nor fear as we depart—
No parting, nothing that will make us start,
But still they live about our doors for ever

When I am sick in bed, my sister comes to me;
She sits down by the hour with thread and needle
To work for someone else—she is so goodhearted—
And sometimes sings a song that pleases me.

The other day she said, “We are very poor
In this house, but we have our treasures still.”
So I asked what they were. She answered simply,
“Love and truth, brother, love and truth.”

author: buchanan_robert
text:
He had gone out one day into the cold spring night,

The first clear night after Christmas, when the snow
Had melted into rain, and all Nature was stirring,
But Nature had not changed or warmed itself with rest,

Nor seemed at ease within herself nor comforted,

As if some ill were near that still remained hidden.

He passed on down along the winding ways of the lane,

When far before, beyond the trees, he heard the sound
Of voices singing, “Oh joy! Oh bliss befall us!”

And anon they came in sight, coming towards

author: buchanan_robert
text:
The wind has gone down, but I see you still
Moving through my room as you did before;

author: cushag
text:
" The lummper's gone, an' he gits me no money.

He leaves my little bit to starve."

Still another:

author: emily_dickinson
text:
I sat in me garden one day
To eat my dinner;—

The sun shone bright on the green hills.
But it didna shine on her!

When the wind blows north or east,

We must have our coats on ;

But when it comes from south or west,

O we can go bare-shoon.

[A third, entitled " The Old Man in His Youth."]

There was once an old man that lived far away,
He was poor, but he didn't care to say;
So when his family wanted him to sell his farm,
And buy them some land where they could settle down,
They told him he ought not to be so foolish,
For he had nothing to live upon

author: cushag
text:
"I've seen you through many a rainy day,
I'll see you to your last," he said;
But now I've got no bread or milk or tea,
Or money on my own good name.

O! there are days when one feels very sad indeed; but then our joys also are great enough to bear all this out, and we can always think of some bright spot in which to take refuge—some little ray of sunshine that may be reflected from the depths below into our hearts as well. We have been accustomed to look up to men, but

author: cushag
text:
Oh, there's a lot o' bother in this here house,
It's very hard to make it nice and clean;
I've been a-washin' all the day long,
But the old things always come up again.

If I had known what work I should get,
The first thing I would have done 'ud be went.

author: emily_dickinson
text: I am so weary that I hardly dare to write a line, but I must do it for the sake of those who may come after me. It is true that I have not been able to leave home much since Christmas; but I was out every day from two or three until five, when we came home, tired as dogs are at nightfall, with nothing left but skin and bones! The last week has been more than ever, even than usual, busy; for some new work has sprung up which required all our strength. As if this were enough, I find that my little girl has

author: john_keats
text:
I am a little flower,
 Grew up on high;
 A long while I bloomed alone
 In sweetest sky;
 But now that spring is here,
 Comes the first fair morn,
 The winds come soft from yonder hill,
 Softly they stir.

Here are two more, with which we will close:

author: emily_dickinson
text:
O let me take a walk alone, 
 To gather flowers for thee;
 The winds are whispering low: "Come, 

Thou wilt not come with me!"

author: emily_dickinson
text:
To be a cloud, to be a bird,
 To rise upon the air;
 So light and fleet as love is fair,
 With never a care!

author: john_keats
john_masefield
text: "I looked at her; she was pale, too. But I did not see her face so much as her eyes. They were large and very dark."

This is our dwelling-place! how pleasant it looks!
What lofty towers are here, what courts immense!
Where shall we rest? where will my mother repose?
The chamber must be chosen for her by us;
For me one of these wide chambers of ease,
That overlooks the broad river—with glass windows.—

author: john_keats
john_keats
text:
But here I must be forced
To stop myself a while;
For after so much toil,
It is not easy to smile,
Or take it for granted
I need but speak again;
Therefore when you think me dead
And laid in my last bed,
Do not disturb me more,
Unless it's to remove
My coffin from before,
That it might stand between
The door and some fresh-made green.

author: john_masefield
text: "I cannot remember where I found it but I am sure that this passage is worthy of study, especially as a fragment of an unfinished autobiography. "The author has always been fond of reading Dickens and now, after thirty years absence from his native country he feels himself impelled by circumstances to return and live in London and at last he writes, 'it seems almost like being born again'. In fact he had lost all self-respect in America when he lived in Boston."

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
"There isn't much of life in it," he said, "For the young men. They leave home for the mines, And the women stay at home or go where they may, If their husbands can get them away. There is nothing For a man to do who has his wits about him, Unless he goes abroad to fight, or takes the law, Or runs the country--or makes money somehow."

And this also from the same source:

author: john_masefield
text:
"Her hands were shaking like leaves in autumn,
While the man spoke that dreadful, dreadful thing
To the woman standing beside him again."

What are the differences between these two pieces?

The first one has a sense of loss ("and I know now why they didn’t keep us all") but also the second is about "a terrible event". Is it possible for both pieces to be true at the same time? If so, how could this be?

author: john_masefield
text:
"The men are standing round him, smoking in silence,
With a great respect for his words as they speak out loud,
But none had heard that she was dying last night.
Her son, who is not here, has spoken about it."

These were published in 1930. Does this imply anything?

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
I am an orphan now, not even a cat,
Not even a rat.

They say you have no need of me. You don’t care
for my songs.

You look down on me because I am too old,
Because I know about many things,

About things which are never spoken of. They
say it is best if we do not talk,

But this makes them all the more eager to
hear about them. . ..

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
This morning I’m thinking about death,
Because my husband died yesterday, after thirty-five years of marriage. It was in my room
that he fell asleep, after all these hours on his feet, and so it is here we shall lay him.

Heard from him on Thursday; he says:

You know we used to have some fun together when we were younger; well, it will be good to see you again in this way. . .”

The world is cruel, indeed, as far as war is concerned—though not always so to those who fight in them.

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text: There is no end to it all . . , . . No beginning, either. But why ask about beginnings and endings when every time something changes everything starts again in the middle, or perhaps it begins somewhere else . . .. It is not a question of an hour passing while we are asleep, nor is it a matter of a day turning into night . . ., neither one nor the other. For it seems that with each step you take, you find yourself on a different road; and yet the roads have no intersections, no crossings. You cannot turn around to return whence you came. Perhaps these

author: kemp_harry_1883_1960
text:
When the moon shines in the evening sky,
I look up and think of what happened in my life

There are so many things about which
To make a song or write a poem . . ,

Or else, one day it will come back

And this time, we won’t let them go!

Yet another one of the same author, written before the war began:

My heart is heavy with pain as I gaze across
The fields of snow where my brothers died;

But still they lived—they did not lie beneath these
Fields of white. They fought and

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
I wish to show you the great deeds that I have done.

Let me see those who know me tell the truth.

author: robert_frost
text:
To suffer, to endure, for the love of a fair maid,

And then not marry her; this is my delight!

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
How oft from morn till night in deep distress

I sought relief among all that could be blessed!

The same author:

With every step I felt his feet go down Into the earth; for when I touched them 'twas as if 1 were touching nothing but the sand. And in this manner he led me four days into the wilderness, without so much as giving me either water to drink or food to eat. (Deut., 32:10)

author: newman_john_henry_1801_1890
text:
Philip's cruel hand dealt him blows so severe
That in that hour his life seemed to expire.

author: robert_frost
text:
"I wonder if you know my mother? She is dead now. But she went about in the fields;
she said, 'God gave me a heart for this work!'. She used to be so kind to me. When I was sick, she would come out with her apron full of grass, and make the bed for me, and take care of me as though I were her own child. The Lord has taken away her strength from her, but He has given her such patience!'

author: stephen_crane
text:
The other day, as they were bringing in the hay,
They asked me if I wouldn't take on one more boy;
"No," says I, "that would put too much burden upon my labour."
But then I said to myself again,
And for good measure said aloud,
It's very awkward now with three or four boys running round,
For their mother must keep house and do all her work,
Which takes up most part of every day;
Of course she has no strength left over for them.
"This child of mine—it all depends on how you look at it. On the whole she seems quite pleasant enough; but then, as my wife says, why couldn't she live in her own way?"

author: robert_frost
text:
"The only work we do without payment
Is in our minds; so all those who know it best
Should not be made to give up their leisure—
No one has been so lucky as myself.
If this had been your fate, then no doubt you would
Have thought me selfish, for my sake I ask
That you should have some share in my pleasure."

author: robert_frost
text: "Well, if you see him coming round here again, I think we'd all best set upon him fast; No one can do as much harm to a man As another man may be tempted to." Note: This poem relates to Thomas Hardy’s father who had no regular occupation but worked for various farmers in the locality where the family lived (Dorchester, Dorset). It appears in The Poems of Thomas Hardy, edited by Harold Williams and published in London, 1923, pp. 560–61.

author: stephen_crane

text:

 Her eyes were tired and weary from toil;
 She closed them all night long.
 She opened them again when it grew day.

The first child she addressed was an only son who had been her devoted companion from childhood. She leaned forward with clasped hands and spoke earnestly: “My son,” she began, “I have always wished for you since I gave birth to you.” But as she continued, she paused every few minutes to wipe away tears which fell fast on her cheeks. author: stephen_crane
text:
There are four kings and two queens;
 Who will take these cards away?
 Four jacks and six knaves.
 There are four pairs of twins.
 How many people would you say there are all told?

author: stephen_crane
text:
The day was old; it had been grey,
 But now there came along a ray,
 And it shot through my window pane,
 Across my carpeted floor,
 To where I sat beside my book,
 Thinking of some things I'd never looked;
 Yet on this happy evening hour
 It shone and brightened up all over me—
 That happy ray from God above!

author: stothert_james_a
text:
When we are gone, how bright will be your home!
How soon shall we there dwell together?
How glad for each the other’s presence comes,
To take their place at table and their rest!
Then let us now be ready, every one,
For work so pleasant—work so perfect too;
For what may come of service such as this,
Of life which ends like this.

author: thomas_hardy
text:
In this pure spirit’s own bright face
My soul hath long found sweet embrace;
It feeds and soothes my every pain
As no one else can do again!

What if we could be but what we are, —
Though only once in time's long flow of years, —


As now a moment in a sunless star ?
Ah! no such magic charm would then appear :

author: stothert_james_a
stothert_james_a
text:
O! you who stand upon the highest height,
And see across this vast abyss of years,
Who have surveyed in a wide vision bright

The past and future of my soul's dear tears;
What words can e'er express your pitying grace?

You know not yet how often I have cried —

author: thomas_hardy
text:
I went down into the forest once,
 To pick the flowers that grew along the ways,
 When I came back a little while ago,
 The roses were all picked, all torn away!
 What must they say?  They are singing now!
 I hear them talk together on the way.

author: william_wordsworth
text:
THEY came who came not; they went who went not;
They spoke not words that were spoken;
Their hands did touch not those hands;
The things of which I dreamed,
Forgetting how dreams end,
Were not fulfilled.
The sun went down before my eyes,
But my soul could still behold it,
And know that it was bright.

Then all seemed well, but not quite so good,
As I had thought; then I was told,
“You shall forget! ” and forgot.

There is a spot on earth
Where flowers are fair and green;
And skies have music stored
That songs can never win;
But spirits which delight
In beauty that hath weight
Are not invited thither
By any earthly sign.

author: thomas_hardy
text:
IT is true that life may be,
 When not all else can give,
 The very thing it needs.
 Its chief delight shall live,
 By faith or reason known,—the soul
 That keeps alive our love for one!

 For some are gifts that bring
 All things but peace; they dwell
 Where hope may hide its wing.
 What if you find your own,
 Who know his heart so well?
 To him your thought may tell.

 But who will look on earth
 And call upon a friend?
 He waits by death's hard threshold;

author: thomas_hardy
text:
The rose is not a rose to you,
 Nor are the daisies white;
 You never thought them pretty blue,
 And yet they look so bright!

author: william_wordsworth
text:
O thou whose eye can pierce beyond our skies,
 O thou, whose presence never leaves us free,
 Come down upon our path from heaven's high height!
 Let all this world behold in thee thy Might,
 And own its sovereign Power, which cannot hide
 Her secret counsels from the most obscure,
 Or suffer wrong, but punish and provide
 The very wrongs themselves. Oh let him come
 Whose hand is stretched to crush us in his power,
 Before whom even the great ones fall like straw,
 Whom none can stop, nor plead, nor pray against,

author: buchanan_robert
text: I never heard such words from human lips, Never, but those of John Milton. They are almost worthy to be written upon his tombstone, which shall some day cover his ashes.

I have been thinking what might possibly happen when all this is over, for the end must come some time. If France succeeds against Germany we shall all be glad enough for our own sakes, but in truth she will scarcely take the trouble to help us; and if Germany wins out of hand—well, then, as sure as fate things would begin to look very bad indeed for poor old England. author: william_wordsworth
text:
The Sun does shine above us still,
 And we are happy in his light.
 We have some cause to bless him still,  
 Though we know him not, though he fight; 
 He is our friend, whatever we may say.

author: william_wordsworth
text:
We are all born so young,
 We die but very old;
 The middle part between
 Is filled with nothing green.

Yet when we have our fill
 Of time that flies too fast,
 It comes again in vain --
 No chance for us at last.
